summary: Defines mechanisms for privacy in SIP. It gives guidelines for building messages that do not reveal personal identity information, defines a privacy service role for intermediaries, and lets users ask for particular privacy functions. It handles needs that user agents cannot satisfy themselves.

eli5.summary: Sometimes you want to call someone without showing your name. This document sets up ways to hide who you are, including a helper in the middle who can erase your details.

subtitle: How SIP users can hide who they are, and how a privacy service in the network helps them do it.

tldr.problem: SIP messages carry identity in many places, such as the From, Contact and Via headers, and some of those headers are needed for routing, so a user agent cannot hide them on its own.
tldr.mechanism: User agents build messages with anonymous values and ask for network help with a new Privacy header (header, session, user, none, critical), while a new logical role called a privacy service removes or replaces the revealing data.
tldr.outcome: Users can get three degrees of privacy, but they must trust the privacy service, and session privacy without end-to-end encryption is NOT RECOMMENDED.

today: RFC 3323 is a Proposed Standard from November 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Privacy in SIP
sections.content:
RFC 3323 defines privacy as withholding a person's identity and related personal information from one or more parties in a SIP dialog, including the destination and any intermediaries. Withholding identity means the other parties cannot send new requests to the user outside the current dialog.

Identity in SIP is usually a SIP URI plus an optional display-name, such as sip:alice@atlanta.com and "Alice", appearing in the To and From headers. It can also leak through the Contact header, and through headers that proxies add, such as Via and Record-Route. A Via header might reveal the service provider a user sends through, which can hint at who the user is.

Two principles guide the design: users are empowered to hide their identity, but intermediaries and designated recipients are entitled to reject requests whose originator cannot be identified. The RFC covers only the headers in the core SIP specification, and does not reconsider confidentiality of headers and bodies or session security.
sections.eli5: Your name tag shows up in several places on a letter and on the envelope. Hiding it everywhere takes both you and the post office.

sections.title: Three Degrees of Privacy
sections.content:
A user may want to hide identity from the final destination but not from intermediaries, from intermediaries but not from the destination, or from both. The RFC describes three degrees: one level of user-provided privacy and two levels of network-provided privacy, called header privacy and session privacy.

User-provided privacy is whatever the user agent can do itself, such as using an anonymous From value or encrypting bodies end to end. If a dialog goes directly end to end, the participants' network addresses cannot be concealed. Some information can only be concealed by an intermediary that is trusted to remove it.

Users are advised not to guess their privacy needs from where they expect a request to go, because a request to a telephone number could be retargeted to a native SIP endpoint. They should also not withhold identity automatically on every message, because proxies and users may refuse requests from parties they cannot identify.
sections.eli5: You can wear a mask yourself, but only a helper can stop the mailman from seeing your return address. Wearing a mask all the time may also make people refuse to talk to you.

sections.title: What a User Agent Does
sections.content:
Headers that can reveal the originator include From, Contact, Reply-To, Via, Call-Info, User-Agent, Organization, Server, Subject, Call-ID, In-Reply-To and Warning. A user agent SHOULD leave out optional headers that could divulge personal information, and SHOULD populate URIs according to the anonymity guidelines. The Call-ID often embeds an IP address or hostname, so user agents SHOULD substitute a suitably long random value.

For anonymity the display-name "Anonymous" is RECOMMENDED, and the hostname anonymous.invalid SHOULD be used for anonymous URIs. The From header MUST still carry a valid and unique tag= parameter.

Headers used to route later requests in the dialog, such as Contact and Via, must hold working values. Their host portion SHOULD NOT be changed by the user agent for privacy reasons. If they need anonymizing, the user asks a privacy service. To hide headers from intermediaries only, the user MAY place the real values in an encapsulated message/sip S/MIME body.
sections.eli5: You can write a fake name on the card you hand out, but your real return address on the envelope must stay readable or replies cannot find you. So you ask a helper to cover it.

sections.title: The Privacy Header
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new SIP header, Privacy, whose values are header, session, user, none, critical or another token. Each value may appear at most once. A Privacy header MUST consist of either none, or one or more of user, header and session, optionally followed by critical.

  • header: the service obscures headers that cannot be cleaned without intermediary help, such as Via and Contact, and adds no revealing headers.
  • session: the service anonymizes the session media, masking the IP address that session traffic comes from. User agents MUST NOT encrypt SDP bodies when asking for this.
  • user: user-level privacy functions must be provided by the network. It is usually set only by intermediaries, though user agents MAY set it on REGISTER requests.
  • none: apply no privacy functions. Intermediaries MUST NOT remove or alter a Privacy header with this value.
  • critical: if the requested services cannot be provided, the request should be rejected.

User agents SHOULD include the header when network privacy is needed. A user agent that sends directly to a privacy service SHOULD add a Proxy-Require header with the option-tag privacy, so a request to a proxy that does not support the extension fails.
sections.eli5: The Privacy header is a sticky note on your letter telling the helper what to cover up: the envelope, the whole conversation, your personal details, or nothing at all.

sections.title: Reaching a Privacy Service
sections.content:
The usual way to invoke a privacy service is to route the request through it, traditionally with pre-loaded Route headers. Service providers are RECOMMENDED to combine the privacy service with a local outbound proxy. A user who wants to hide their local administrative domain must use a third-party anonymization service outside the domains involved in the session.

Using TLS or similar network or transport security to the privacy service is highly RECOMMENDED. Ideally the user makes a direct connection with a single pre-loaded Route header, which lets the user check a certificate and stops intermediaries from removing the privacy request. Otherwise SIPS should be used.

Responses follow the same path as requests, so a responder cannot add a privacy service afterward. Instead the user can ensure requests reach them through one, for example by getting an anonymous callback URI from a third-party service, by sending REGISTER requests through a privacy service with user privacy so it inserts anonymous Contact URIs, or by using a CPL script. Privacy services MAY pass requests to other privacy services.
sections.eli5: To use the helper, you hand your letter to them first. For replies, you give out the helper's address as yours, so the answers come through the helper too.

sections.title: What a Privacy Service Does
sections.content:
The privacy service is a new logical role, usually played by a proxy-like intermediary. It supplies privacy functions that user agents cannot. It SHOULD evaluate the Privacy header and usually apply only the requested services, though it MAY use a pre-arranged user profile. If the value is none, it MUST NOT perform any privacy function or modify the header.

Privacy services MUST support none and critical, and MAY support the other levels. If critical is present and the service cannot do everything requested, it MUST fail the request with a 500 (Server Error) response. After performing a function it SHOULD remove the matching value from the Privacy header, and when the last value is gone the whole header MUST be removed, along with the privacy option-tag in Proxy-Require.

Header privacy: the service must often act as a transparent back-to-back user agent (B2BUA). It SHOULD NOT add revealing headers such as Call-Info, Server or Organization, SHOULD strip earlier Via headers and add a single Via of its own, and SHOULD replace Contact with a URI that dereferences to the service. It SHOULD also strip Record-Route headers, and must remember the removed values per dialog so it can restore them later.

Session privacy: the service MUST act as a B2BUA and control a middlebox that provides an apparent source and sink for session traffic. How is outside the RFC's scope.

User privacy: the service MUST remove non-essential headers such as Subject, Call-Info, Organization, User-Agent, Reply-To and In-Reply-To. It may change the From header and may modify Call-ID. When it changes dialog-matching headers it SHOULD act as a transparent B2BUA and MUST restore the former values in messages sent to the originating user agent.
sections.eli5: The helper takes your letter, covers up your details with its own address, and remembers the real ones. When a reply comes back, it puts your real address back so you get it.

sections.title: Trust and Security
sections.content:
Messages that request privacy need both confidentiality and integrity. Without integrity, the requested functions could be downgraded or removed. Without confidentiality, eavesdroppers could see exactly the information the user wants hidden.

All network-provided privacy requires a good deal of trust in the privacy service, so users should only trust services that are accountable to them. Requesting session privacy without end-to-end security for the media, such as SRTP for RTP, is NOT RECOMMENDED, because the anonymizer itself becomes party to the communication. For downstream parties, the privacy service is the only source to which anonymous messages can be traced.

Authentication, including Digest, is outside the scope of the privacy mechanism. Users who do not want to reveal identity to a server that challenges them MAY choose not to respond.
sections.eli5: The helper can see everything, so you must pick one you trust and keep your talking secret from the helper too.

items.label: Header privacy
items.desc: Obscure headers such as Via and Contact that the user cannot clean alone.

items.label: No privacy
items.desc: Services must not perform any privacy function.

items.label: Critical
items.desc: Perform the services or fail the request.
